---
title: "Dead Ends?"
body-classes: page-small
---

Work that has not reached publication: studies I designed and did not run,
analyses that stalled, and tools I built and stopped using. The published record
makes research look far tidier than it is.

## Analyses

### Emotion dynamics as the mechanism linking academic adversity to internalizing symptoms

*Presented as a poster at ISSBD 2026, Incheon. Manuscript paused.*

The interesting result is the one I did not predict. Patterns usually described
as maladaptive looked protective under adversity: low negative-affect
differentiation buffered cumulative stress on anxiety, high negative-affect
instability buffered immediate stress on both depression and anxiety, and low
positive-affect inertia was protective against immediate stress on anxiety.
Negative-affect intensity did behave as expected, mediating stress to both
outcomes.

::: {.field}
[Idea]{.k}
Academic stress is a salient adolescent adversity. I asked whether emotion
dynamics function as the adaptation process connecting it to internalizing
symptoms, through two competing routes: coping with adversity drains the
cognitive resources regulation requires, or adaptive regulation patterns buffer
the stressor. Four dynamics were examined: intensity, instability, inertia, and
differentiation.
:::

::: {.field}
[Analysis]{.k}
Dynamic structural equation modelling in Mplus to derive the person-level
dynamic indices, then structural equation models testing mediation and
moderation. Sensitivity battery run alongside the main models: without
controls, with controls entered separately for anxiety and for depression, and
with the full interaction specification.
:::

::: {.field}
[Participants]{.k}
271 adolescents from a longitudinal study in the southern United States, 38% in
7th grade and 62% in 8th, 56% female. 47% Latinx, 19% White, 11% Asian, 5%
Black, 18% other.
:::

::: {.field}
[Measures]{.k}
Three annual surveys measuring cumulative academic stress and depressive and
anxiety symptoms, plus a 14-day daily diary measuring daily academic stress and
positive and negative affect. Dynamic indices computed from the diary series.
:::

### Peer synchrony and self-regulation in early childhood

*Designed and drafted through several rounds in late 2023. Never run.*

::: {.field}
[Idea]{.k}
Caregiver-child synchrony is well studied; synchrony between young peers is
not. I proposed that peer synchrony plays a similar but distinct role in how
self-regulation develops, extending the biobehavioural model to contexts outside
the family and treating preschoolers as agents shaping their own interactions
rather than only recipients of caregiving.
:::

::: {.field}
[Analysis]{.k}
Planned: multilevel models estimating physiological synchrony as the effect of
one randomly assigned partner's RSA on the other's, then two-sample t-tests or
Mann-Whitney U tests comparing friend and unfamiliar dyads on synchrony
strength, duration of behavioural synchrony, and self-regulation behaviour.
:::

::: {.field}
[Participants]{.k}
Planned: 30 same-gender peer dyads, 60 children aged 3 to 5 years, with half
randomly assigned to interact with a friend and half with an unfamiliar peer.
:::

::: {.field}
[Measures]{.k}
RSA recorded simultaneously from both children during a 5-minute cooperative
challenge task, used to estimate physiological synchrony; behavioural synchrony
coded from video; observed self-regulation behaviour.
:::

## Tools

### An automated literature-review pipeline

*Version 1.0, unmaintained, and overtaken.*

::: {.field}
[Idea]{.k}
Screening for a systematic review is mechanical and error-prone in a way that
seemed automatable: take exported search results, fill the metadata gaps, and
triage abstracts against inclusion criteria so a human only adjudicates the
ambiguous ones.
:::

::: {.field}
[Built]{.k}
An R pipeline that ingested CSV exports from LitSift, combined them across
searches, and recovered missing abstracts from the CrossRef API by DOI, with
per-record error handling so one bad response could not kill a run. Abstract
coverage improved substantially over the raw exports.
:::

I am listing this less as a failure than as something the ground moved under.
It got as far as metadata completion and stalled before screening, which is the
part that matters. That gap is exactly what general-purpose agents now close,
and they do it without a bespoke pipeline. The useful work left is not building
the tool but deciding what it has to prove before anyone trusts it: hand-screen
a few hundred abstracts, then require any automated screener to reproduce those
decisions at a measured rate. That reframes the project from writing a pipeline
to measuring agreement, which is both more tractable and more publishable, and
it is the version I would still like to do.
